movements.name: St Thomas Christians, 1300-1517
movements.legacy: The community is still here. After 1517 came pressure from the Portuguese. Then came the Synod of Diamper in 1599 and the Coonan Cross revolt of 1653. Between them, these split the St Thomas Christians into the several churches they are now. They include the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics, the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian churches, the Mar Thoma Church and others. Together they have several million members, in Kerala and far beyond. Syriac is still used when they worship. The texts of this era already take it as known that the apostle Thomas founded the church. That is still how the community sees itself.

documentedStories.title: Four Bishops Write Home from Malabar
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Sent from Mesopotamia to a church that had been without a bishop for decades, the new Syriac bishops of India write to their patriarch in the Hakkari mountains describing thirty thousand Christian families, churches at Cranganore and Quilon, and ships from a Christian nation no one has heard of.
documentedStories.text: Around 1490 the St Thomas Christians of Malabar, whose last bishops from Mesopotamia had died, sent three men to find the patriarch of the Church of the East, now living in a monastery near Gazarta on the Tigris after Timur’s wars. In 1504 the bishops in India — Mar Yahballaha, Mar Denha, Mar Jacob and Mar Thomas — wrote to the new patriarch Eliya V, and their letter survives in Syriac. They describe the journey: to Hormuz, by ship to Cannanore, on to Cranganore, the reception by the Christians ‘with great joy’, the churches they consecrated and the ordinations they performed. They estimate the community at about thirty thousand families in some twenty towns, ‘rich and honoured’, with their own headman, living among Hindus and Muslims under Hindu rulers; they describe the pepper trade and the church at Quilon. Then, near the end, they report news: ‘powerful ships’ had arrived from the west, from a nation called Portugal, whose people were Christians and had a bishop with them, who had received the Syriac bishops kindly and celebrated the liturgy with them at Cannanore, and who were building a fortress and fighting the Muslims of Calicut. The letter is the last document of the St Thomas Christians as a church of the East before the Portuguese began, within a generation, to bring them under Rome; the men who wrote it did not know that, and it is also the only description of the Malabar church by its own bishops before 1500.
documentedStories.caveat: The letter is authentic and preserved in a Syriac manuscript in the Vatican; its numbers are round. The bishops’ favorable first impression of the Portuguese is their own and predates the Synod of Diamper by ninety-five years.

movements.name: The Anabaptist Movements
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base, read with care for genre — the Martyrs Mirror and the Hutterite Chronicle alongside the movement's own hymnody. Its court testimonies are coerced, not plain inside voice. Its window ends in 1650, bringing the Dordrecht Confession (1632) back inside its own window.

documentedStories.title: Dirk Willems Turns Back on the Ice
documentedStories.teaser: An Anabaptist escaping across a frozen moat at Asperen hears the man chasing him break through the ice, goes back, and pulls him out. He is arrested on the spot and burned.
documentedStories.text: Dirk Willems had been rebaptized at Rotterdam, had let others be rebaptized in his house at Asperen in Holland, and was under sentence when he escaped from the town’s prison by a rope of knotted rags and ran across the moat, which was frozen. The Martyrs Mirror, the great Dutch Mennonite compilation of 1660, gives the story and the court record. A thief-catcher — a guard set to pursue him — followed onto the ice, which had borne the starved prisoner and did not bear the guard; he broke through. Willems, on the far bank, heard him and turned back and pulled him out. The guard, the account says, wanted to let him go; the burgomaster standing on the bank called out that he should remember his oath, and the guard arrested the man who had saved him. The sentence of the Asperen court, dated 16 May 1569, is printed: Dirk Willems, having ‘persisted obstinately in his opinion’, rebaptized and having permitted rebaptism in his house, is to be executed by fire. The Martyrs Mirror adds that the wind carried the flames away from him so that he died slowly, crying out seventy times ‘O my Lord, my God’, until the bailiff, sickened, ordered him despatched. The Mennonites and Amish have kept the story and the engraving of it — the man on the ice reaching down — as the picture of what their faith requires, which is not to escape.
documentedStories.caveat: The court sentence is authentic and reproduced by van Braght from the Asperen records; the narrative of the rescue comes from the same compilation, made ninety years later from earlier martyr books, and has no contemporary independent witness. The detail of the seventy cries is hagiographic.

documentedStories.title: The Kingdom at Münster
documentedStories.teaser: Anabaptists take control of a Westphalian city, expel or rebaptize everyone, abolish money, introduce polygamy under a tailor who crowns himself king of the New Jerusalem, and are starved, betrayed and slaughtered — and every other Anabaptist pays for it.
documentedStories.text: Münster had elected an Anabaptist-leaning council in February 1534 under the preacher Bernhard Rothmann, and within weeks Dutch followers of the prophet Melchior Hoffman’s successor Jan Matthijs had arrived and taken it over. Those who would not be rebaptized were driven out of the gates into the snow; property was declared common and money abolished; books other than the Bible were burned. The prince-bishop besieged the city. Matthijs, who had declared it the New Jerusalem, rode out against the besiegers on Easter Day with a handful of men, believing himself invulnerable, and was killed. Jan van Leiden, a tailor from Leiden, took his place, ran naked through the streets in prophecy, dissolved the council, introduced polygamy — he took sixteen wives, and beheaded one in the market square himself — and in September had himself crowned king of the whole world, with a court and a throne. In June 1535 the city was betrayed to the besiegers and most of its defenders killed. Jan van Leiden and two lieutenants were tortured with hot tongs before the crowd in January 1536, and their bodies hung in cages from the tower of St Lambert’s, where the cages still are. Menno Simons, who left his priesthood the following year, wrote against ‘the abomination of Münster’ for the rest of his life; the peaceful Anabaptists who became the Mennonites were hunted for two generations as if they had been there. The tradition has never been allowed to forget it, and has not tried to.
documentedStories.caveat: Gresbeck’s eyewitness account and Kerssenbrock’s later history are hostile; Rothmann’s own pamphlets from inside the city survive and confirm the doctrines. The sixteen wives and the beheading rest on the hostile accounts and on the trial confessions, which were extracted under torture. The outline is not disputed.

movements.name: The English Reformation & Elizabethan Settlement
movements.relationsSummary: Shaped by Lutheran and Reformed influences taking root in England. It carried on as the Church of England, and its Puritan wing gave rise to the churches that later broke away. Its story runs through the Stuart century, from the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 to the Westminster Assembly.

movements.name: Puritanism
movements.longDescription: Puritans were the English Protestants who thought the Elizabethan settlement had stopped halfway. That a church with bishops, surplices and a set liturgy still carried too much of what the Reformation was meant to clear away. Their real distinctiveness lay less in church furniture than in the inner life. They kept diaries, examined their own hearts in writing, and made the conversion narrative — an account of how God had brought you to faith, told aloud before a congregation. A normal thing for ordinary men and women to produce. Pressed at home, thousands sailed for New England from 1630. Those who stayed came to dominate the Long Parliament and the Westminster Assembly, and after the Restoration of 1660 were ejected from the Church of England altogether.

documentedStories.title: Jeremias II Asks the Lutherans to Stop Writing
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The theologians of Tübingen send the patriarch of Constantinople a Greek translation of the Augsburg Confession, hoping for recognition. After three exchanges of long letters he tells them, courteously, to go their own way and write to him only as friends.
documentedStories.text: In 1573 the Lutheran chaplain of the imperial embassy at Constantinople, Stephan Gerlach, carried letters from Jakob Andreae and Martin Crusius of Tübingen to the patriarch Jeremias II, with a Greek version of the Augsburg Confession, asking for his judgment. The Lutherans hoped that the ancient church of the East, free of the pope, would recognize their teaching as its own. His First Answer of 1576 goes through the Confession article by article — accepting some, correcting others, and rejecting justification by faith alone, the denial of free will, the removal of the invocation of saints and the reduction of the sacraments — in the voice of a church that had not been asked its opinion for a century and meant to give it fully. The Tübingen theologians replied; he answered again in 1579, more shortly; they replied again; and in 1581 he wrote the Third Answer, which ends the correspondence: ‘We ask you not to trouble us further, nor to write to us on these matters. Go your own way; but write to us, if you wish, for friendship’s sake.’ The Lutherans printed the whole exchange in 1584 — with the patriarch’s refusals — and the Catholics reprinted it with glee. The letters are the first sustained encounter between the Reformation and Orthodoxy, and the Orthodox side is the voice of a captive church declining to be recruited by either western party: not Rome, not Wittenberg, and no further letters, please.
documentedStories.caveat: The correspondence is authentic and was printed by the Tübingen side in 1584 with both parties’ texts; Jeremias’ answers were drafted with the help of his synod’s theologians. The Orthodox church has treated the Answers as a confessional document, though they were letters.

documentedStories.title: Cyril Lucaris Is Strangled on a Boat
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The patriarch who has been deposed and restored five times, whose Confession reads like Geneva’s, and whom the Jesuits and the Dutch ambassador have fought over for twenty years, is taken from the patriarchate by janissaries on the sultan’s order and killed in the Bosporus.
documentedStories.text: Cyril Lucaris had been educated at Padua and Venice, had spent years in Poland fighting the Union of Brest, and as patriarch of Constantinople from 1620 had allied himself with the Protestant embassies — English and Dutch — against the French and Austrian ambassadors and the Jesuits, who worked to depose him. In 1629 a Confession of Faith appeared in Geneva under his name, in Latin, teaching predestination, justification by faith, two sacraments, and the authority of Scripture over the church; he never publicly repudiated it, and a Greek version with his signature exists. His enemies used it. Deposed and restored five times as the embassies bribed the Porte in turn, he was finally denounced to the sultan Murad IV in June 1638, as the army left for Baghdad, as having incited the Cossacks against the empire. On 27 June janissaries took him from the patriarchate to a boat, and — the Dutch ambassador’s and the Greek accounts agree — strangled him and threw the body into the Bosporus; it was recovered by fishermen and buried by his supporters. Within three months his successor, Cyril Kontaris, held a synod that anathematized him and the Confession by name; synods at Jassy in 1642 and Jerusalem in 1672 did it again. Kontaris was himself strangled by the Ottomans the following year. The Orthodox church has never agreed whether Lucaris wrote the Confession, and has kept the anathemas and, in some quarters, his memory as a martyr, at the same time.
documentedStories.caveat: The manner of death is reported by the Dutch resident Cornelis Haga and by Greek sources and is not disputed; the immediate cause of the denunciation is. Lucaris’ authorship of the Confession is contested by Orthodox historians and generally accepted by others; the page states the dispute.

movements.longDescription: The Christians of the Malabar coast traced their church to the apostle Thomas. For centuries they had worshipped in Syriac and taken their bishops from the Church of the East. The Portuguese found this puzzling and then intolerable. In 1599 Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes held a synod at Diamper. It placed the community under Latin rule, revised its liturgy, and ordered its Syriac books corrected or burned. Half a century of resentment came to a head on 3 January 1653. At Mattancherry a crowd swore they would no longer obey the Jesuits or the Jesuit archbishop, Francisco Garcia. Tradition says they tied ropes to a stone cross as they swore. This is the Coonan Cross Oath, named for a cross said to have bent under the strain.
voices: Aleixo de Menezes — Archbishop of Goa, who convened the Synod of Diamper in 1599
Archdeacon Thomas (Mar Thoma I) — the community's own leader, made bishop by his own people after the 1653 oath
Ahatallah — the Syrian bishop whose disappearance in Portuguese custody helped trigger the revolt of 1653
movements.legacy: The division made in 1653 is still the shape of Christianity in Kerala. Those who returned to Rome became the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church, now one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches in the world. Those who did not are the ancestors of the Malankara Orthodox, Jacobite, Mar Thoma and related churches. All of them still worship in liturgies descended from the Syriac tradition Diamper set out to correct, and the bent cross at Mattancherry is still there.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop Who Never Arrived, and the Oath at the Bent Cross
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Syrian bishop claiming to be sent to the Christians of India is held by the Portuguese, shipped past the crowd waiting for him at Cochin, and vanishes. Within weeks the community swears at a stone cross that it will obey no Jesuit again, and makes its own archdeacon a bishop.
documentedStories.text: In 1652 a Syrian bishop calling himself Ignatius Ahatallah reached Mylapore on the Coromandel coast, claiming that he had been sent as patriarch of the Christians of India. Who had sent him is still argued: he had made a Catholic profession at Rome twenty years earlier, had since served the Syrian and the Coptic patriarchs, and carried letters whose authority the Portuguese refused to recognize. Two Malabar deacons on pilgrimage at Mylapore met him and carried his letter home, and the community received it with joy. The Portuguese put him on a ship for Goa. When it called at Cochin the Thomas Christians, said to have gathered in thousands, asked to see him and were refused; the ship sailed on, and word spread through the churches that he had been drowned in the harbor, or burned by the Inquisition at Goa. On 3 January 1653 a crowd gathered at the stone cross outside the church at Mattancherry and swore, hands on ropes tied to the cross, that they would no longer obey the Jesuit archbishop Francisco Garcia or any Jesuit. In May, at Alangad, twelve priests laid hands on Archdeacon Thomas and named him Mar Thoma, citing a letter attributed to Ahatallah that authorized it. Ahatallah himself was shipped on toward Lisbon and disappears from the record; the likeliest account has him dying in Europe in 1654 without reaching Rome.
documentedStories.caveat: The contemporary accounts are Jesuit and Carmelite, written by the parties the oath was sworn against; the wording of the oath comes from the community's own tradition in variant forms. Ahatallah's commission and his death are both uncertain, and the letter said to authorize the archdeacon's consecration is widely thought not to be his. What is not in doubt is the oath, the date and the consecration.

documentedStories.title: Diamper: The Synod That Burned the Books
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An archbishop from Goa gathers the priests and elders of the Thomas Christians for a week, declares their patriarch a heretic, rewrites their sacraments and orders their Syriac books burned or corrected. Much of what is known about the community before that week is what the synod condemned.
documentedStories.text: Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa arrived in Malabar early in 1599 with soldiers, money and a determination that the Thomas Christians should have no bishop but one Rome sent. Through the spring he toured their churches, confirming and ordaining, on the reasoning that priests who owed their orders to him would owe him obedience. The Archdeacon George, who had governed the community since the death of its last East Syrian bishop, resisted, was threatened with excommunication and with Portuguese pressure on the pepper trade, and submitted. The synod met at Udayamperur, which the Portuguese called Diamper, from 20 to 26 June 1599, with some 150 priests and more than 600 lay representatives. Its decrees, read in Portuguese and Malayalam, declared the patriarch of the East a heretic, condemned the prayers for Nestorius and Theodore, imposed Latin discipline on clerical marriage, fasting and the sacraments, and ordered a list of Syriac books — the Nomocanon, the Book of the Fathers, the homilies of Narsai among them — to be burned or corrected. Menezes then made a second circuit collecting manuscripts, and many were burned at the churches where they were found. The chronicler Gouvea, who wrote the archbishop's official account, presents this as rescue. The modern editor of the acts has shown that the printed decrees include material the assembly never voted on. Much of what is known about the community's worship before 1599 is what the synod condemned.
documentedStories.caveat: The acts and Gouvea's Jornada are the victor's records and describe the community chiefly as a set of errors. That the printed decrees differ from what the assembly approved is the argument of Jonas Thaliath (1958), accepted by most later scholars but disputed in detail. The scale of the burning is known from the order and from later absence, not from an inventory.

movements.longDescription: In 1596 most of the Orthodox bishops of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth met at Brest and accepted communion with Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy, their Church Slavonic, their calendar and their married clergy. Their opponents met in the same town at the same time and rejected it outright, so what the union produced was not one church but two rival hierarchies claiming the same people and arguing in print for a century. The new church had to explain itself constantly — to Rome, to the Orthodox it had left, and to Latin bishops who never quite treated it as an equal. And that argument became the ordinary condition of its life rather than an occasional crisis. Its most famous figure, Archbishop Josaphat Kuntsevych, was killed by a hostile crowd at Vitebsk in 1623.

documentedStories.title: Vitebsk, 12 November 1623
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Catholic chancellor writes to a Uniate archbishop that his closing of Orthodox churches has made a scarecrow of the union. Eighteen months later a crowd kills the archbishop and throws his body in the river; the king's commissioners behead nineteen townsmen and pull down the town hall.
documentedStories.text: Josaphat Kuntsevych became archbishop of Polotsk in 1618, a monk of austere life and a preacher the Orthodox had once crowded to hear, and set about bringing his diocese into the Union of Brest by closing the churches of priests who would not conform. In March 1622 the Lithuanian chancellor Lew Sapieha, a Catholic and a supporter of the union, wrote to him that his methods were losing the cause: the churches of Mogilev and Orsha were sealed, the Orthodox were holding services in fields and barns, the Cossacks were threatening war over it, and the union had been made a scarecrow. Josaphat answered that he was defending what the law gave him. On 12 November 1623 he was at Vitebsk, where his men had arrested an Orthodox priest; the town bells rang, a crowd broke into the archbishop's house, and Josaphat, going out to them, was struck with a halberd and shot, and his body was dragged through the streets and thrown into the Dvina. The king's commission arrived in January 1624: nineteen townsmen were beheaded, the town hall was demolished, and Vitebsk lost its charter of self-government and its bells. Josaphat was beatified in 1643 on the testimony gathered then. The Orthodox archbishop of the same city, Meletij Smotryc'kyj, whom the Uniates blamed for inciting the town, left for Constantinople and Jerusalem, and came back four years later a Uniate.
documentedStories.caveat: The fullest account of the killing is the beatification process, taken from Josaphat's side; Sapieha's letter is authentic and shows that the Uniate leadership itself thought the archbishop's coercion had provoked the town. Both the coercion and the murder are attested; who threw the first stone in the long quarrel is not a question the sources settle.

documentedStories.title: The Lament, and the Man Who Wrote It
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young teacher publishes the Orthodox Church's lament for the noble houses that have left her, and the king orders it burned. Seventeen years later, now an archbishop, he joins the union he had wept over, and a council makes him watch his new book torn up.
documentedStories.text: In 1610 the Vilnius Orthodox brotherhood press issued a Polish book called Threnos, the Lament of the One Holy Universal Apostolic Eastern Church, under the name Theophil Ortholog. Its author was Meletij Smotryc'kyj, a young teacher in the brotherhood school. The book is a widow's lament: the Church speaks as a mother stripped of her robes and her children, and names them — the Ostroz'kyj, Sluc'kyj, Zbaraz'kyj, Wiśniowiecki and dozens of other houses who had gone over to Rome or to the Reformed. ‘Where are those priceless jewels of my crown?’ King Sigismund III ordered the book burned and the brotherhood's printer imprisoned; Uniates answered it in print; the Orthodox read it aloud, and his later Uniate biographer says they had it laid in their coffins. In 1620 Smotryc'kyj was secretly consecrated Orthodox archbishop of Polotsk, the see Josaphat Kuntsevych held for the union, and after Josaphat's murder he left for the Christian East. He returned in 1626 doubting whether the Greek patriarchs still taught what he had defended, and in 1627 he privately joined the union. In 1628 he published an Apology asking the Orthodox to follow him. A council at Kyiv that August made him stand while his book was torn up and its pages trodden underfoot; he signed a recantation and, back at his monastery at Derman', withdrew it and denounced the council. He died a Uniate in 1633.
documentedStories.caveat: Both books and the acts of the Kyiv council of 1628 survive; the accounts of the council scene are partisan on both sides. What Smotryc'kyj believed at each stage is the subject of a large literature, and his own explanations changed. The Orthodox went on reading the Threnos after its author had left them.

movements.name: The Kyiv-Mohyla Orthodox Revival
movements.relationsSummary: Orthodoxy answering Reformation/Counter-Reformation pressure with its own confessional formation; the response to the Union of Brest.
movements.why: Orthodox Kyiv answered the Union of Brest not with a lament but with a school: a lay brotherhood founded a college in 1615, and Metropolitan Petro Mohyla built it on the Jesuit model — Latin, rhetoric, philosophy, theology — on the reasoning that a church cannot defend itself against arguments it cannot read. He also gave the church its own confession of faith and a service book, the Trebnyk of 1646, that fixed how priests actually celebrated the sacraments.
movements.longDescription: Orthodox Kyiv answered the Union of Brest not with a lament but with a school. A lay brotherhood founded one in 1615, and Petro Mohyla, metropolitan from 1633, turned it into a college on the Jesuit model — Latin, rhetoric, philosophy, theology. On the reasoning that a church cannot defend itself against arguments it cannot read. He also gave the Kyivan church its own instruments. An Orthodox Confession of faith, approved in revised form by a council at Iaşi in 1642, a short catechism, and a great service book, the Trebnyk of 1646, which regularized how priests were actually to celebrate the sacraments. It is the clearest case anywhere of a tradition taking up its rivals' tools in order to remain itself.

documentedStories.title: Feed for the Sturgeon of the Dnieper
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Kyiv's Orthodox open a school on the Jesuit model and the Cossacks conclude the teachers are secret Uniates. The prefect writes that there was a time when they made their confessions expecting to be thrown in the river.
documentedStories.text: When Petro Mohyla, then archimandrite of the Kyiv Caves monastery, opened a school at the monastery in 1631 with Latin as its language and the Jesuit colleges as its model, the reaction in Kyiv was not gratitude. The Cossacks and the burghers who had defended Orthodoxy against the union for a generation could not see the difference between a Latin school and a Latin church, and word went round that the teachers were secret Uniates. Sylvester Kossov, the school's prefect, wrote three years later that there had been a time when he and his colleagues, having made their confessions, expected at any moment to be seized and used to feed the sturgeon of the Dnieper, or to be burned. It took the intervention of the brotherhood and the Cossack hetman to make the school safe, and in 1632 it was merged with the brotherhood's own school on the Podil as a compromise, under the brotherhood's oversight and Mohyla's protection. Kossov's Exegesis of 1635 was written to answer the charge that Latin schooling was foreign to Orthodoxy: without Latin, he wrote, Orthodox children would be fools before the courts, the Diet and their Catholic neighbors, and would go to the Jesuits for what their own church could not give them. He became metropolitan of Kyiv himself in 1647, and the college outlived the Commonwealth.
documentedStories.caveat: The threat is known from Kossov's own retrospective account, written in the college's defense, and may be heightened; that the school was suspected and that its merger with the brotherhood school was a political settlement is agreed. The sturgeon are Kossov's image.

documentedStories.title: Digging Up the Church of the Tithes
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A metropolitan clears the rubble of Kyiv's first stone church, four centuries after the Mongols left it, and announces that he has found the bones of the prince who baptized Rus'.
documentedStories.text: Kyiv in Mohyla's time was a city of ruins, with the churches of the Kyivan princes lying broken since the Mongol sack of 1240 and several of the best preserved in Uniate hands. Mohyla made their recovery a program. He regained St Sophia from the Uniates in 1633 and began repairing it; he rebuilt the Church of the Saviour at Berestove; and in 1635 he had the rubble of the Church of the Tithes, Vladimir's first stone church, cleared, and announced that among the foundations two sarcophagi had been found, one of them holding the remains of St Vladimir himself. He took the skull and other bones, placed the skull in the Dormition cathedral of the Caves monastery, sent a jawbone to the tsar in Moscow, and built a small church over the site. The monastery's press published the finds in the Teraturgema of 1638, a catalog of the monastery's miracles by the monk Afanasij Kal'nofojs'kyj, which set out, with maps, what Kyiv had been. Historians doubt the identification, and the bones were dispersed after 1917. What is not in doubt is what Mohyla was doing: giving the Orthodox of the Commonwealth back the city of their baptism, in stone, as an answer to the argument, made by Uniate and Catholic polemicists alike, that theirs was a church without a past.
documentedStories.caveat: The excavation and the announcement are contemporary and documented; the identification of the remains as Vladimir's rests on Mohyla's word and is not accepted by modern archaeology. The Teraturgema is a miracle-book with a program, and reads as one.

sources.note: The Caves monastery's miracle-book, with the account of the finds and the plans of Kyiv.

movements.name: The Remonstrants and Dort
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Remonstrance of 1610, the acts and canons of the Synod of Dort, Simon Episcopius's writings, and the exile Brotherhood's own records.
movements.relationsSummary: The sharpest internal contest inside Reformed Protestantism in this era: the Five Articles of 1610, judged and condemned by the Synod of Dort in 1618-19, about two hundred ministers deposed, and the Remonstrant Brotherhood driven into exile until toleration returned in the 1630s. The Brotherhood continued afterward with its own seminary in Amsterdam, later associated with the theologian Philipp van Limborch.
movements.why: After Jacobus Arminius raised doubts about how strictly predestination should be taught, his followers set out five articles in the Remonstrance of 1610 — a quarrel that swallowed Dutch politics and sent the statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt to the scaffold in 1619. The Synod of Dort answered with five canons of its own, deposing some two hundred ministers, until toleration returned in the 1630s and the exiles came home to build a church of their own.
movements.longDescription: The Dutch Reformed minister Jacobus Arminius had doubts about how strictly predestination should be taught, and after his death in 1609 his supporters set them out in five articles — the Remonstrance of 1610. Asking the government to allow their view. The quarrel that followed swallowed the young Dutch Republic, mixing theology with politics until it ended on a scaffold. The statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, the Remonstrants' protector, was executed in 1619. The Synod of Dort, meeting through the winter of 1618-19 with delegates from Reformed churches across Europe, condemned the Remonstrance and answered it with five canons of its own. Some two hundred ministers were deposed and their leaders driven into exile — until toleration returned in the 1630s and they came home to build a church of their own.
voices: Jacobus Arminius — Leiden professor whose questions about predestination began the controversy
Simon Episcopius — the Remonstrants' spokesman at Dort and chief theologian of the church they built in exile
Hugo Grotius — jurist and Remonstrant sympathizer, imprisoned for his part in the affair and famously smuggled out in a book chest
Johan van Oldenbarnevelt — the Republic's leading statesman and the Remonstrants' protector, executed in 1619
movements.legacy: Both sides outlived the quarrel. The Remonstrant Brotherhood is still a small Dutch church, with its own seminary in Amsterdam. The Canons of Dort became one of the three Dutch Reformed standards of faith. Ministers swore to them as far away as North America. 'Arminian' became a lasting label in English theology. John Wesley took it up a century later, and the whole Methodist family took it from him.

experienceToday.text: The Grote Kerk in Dordrecht — where the Synod of Dort opened and closed, with a permanent exhibition about it in the south aisle chapels

documentedStories.title: ‘Dimittimini, Exite!’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Summoned to the Synod of Dort as defendants rather than delegates, the Remonstrants spend five weeks arguing about who may set the order of debate. The president ends it by telling them they began with a lie and end with one, and orders them out. An English observer writes home that the foreign divines were dismayed.
documentedStories.text: The Synod of Dort opened on 13 November 1618 with delegates from the Dutch provinces and from the Reformed churches of England, Scotland, the Palatinate, Switzerland, Hesse, Bremen, Emden and Geneva; the French delegates had been forbidden by their king to come. The Remonstrants were not delegates. Thirteen of them, led by Simon Episcopius, professor at Leiden, were summoned as parties to answer for their doctrine, and arrived on 6 December. The next day Episcopius delivered an oration of nearly two hours, in Latin, defending the Remonstrants' right to state their whole position and to argue against unconditional reprobation first, since it was what the people feared. The synod's president, Johannes Bogerman, insisted that they answer the synod's questions in the synod's order. For five weeks the two sides argued procedure. On 14 January 1619 Bogerman lost patience and, in a speech that the English observer John Hales reported home, told them that they had begun with a lie and ended with one, that they were unworthy of the synod's patience, and concluded, ‘Dimittimini, exite!’ — ‘You are dismissed, go!’ Hales wrote that the foreign delegates disliked the manner of it. The synod went on to judge the Remonstrant doctrine from their writings, and its Canons were read in the Great Church on 6 May 1619. The Remonstrant ministers who would not sign an Act of Cessation were banished in July; some two hundred were deposed. Episcopius went to Antwerp and wrote the confession of the church they founded there.
documentedStories.caveat: Hales's letters are a contemporary eyewitness record by a member of the English delegation's household, and the Acta confirm the dates; the exact words of Bogerman's speech are as Hales and the Remonstrants reported them. The Canons of Dort say nothing about the manner of the dismissal.

sources.note: Eyewitness letters to the English ambassador, including the dismissal of 14 January.

sources.note: The synod's own record and its decisions.

documentedStories.title: A Brotherhood in Exile, and a Church That Could Not Be Seen from the Street
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The banished ministers meet at Antwerp and agree to be a society rather than a church, slip back over the border under false names to preach in barns, and, when Amsterdam relents, build a meeting-house for a thousand people behind a row of ordinary house fronts.
documentedStories.text: The banished ministers gathered at Antwerp, in the Spanish Netherlands, in the autumn of 1619, and at the end of September constituted themselves as a Brotherhood — not a church, they said, since they did not wish to add to the divisions of the Reformed, but a society of ministers who would serve congregations wherever they could. Johannes Uytenbogaert, the old court preacher who had drafted the Remonstrance of 1610, presided; Episcopius wrote the Confession of 1621, which set out the Remonstrant faith and insisted that no confession should bind consciences. For a decade the Brotherhood's ministers slipped in and out of the Republic under assumed names, preached in barns and private houses, and were fined, imprisoned and, in a few cases, sent to the fortress at Loevestein; congregations were broken up by soldiers and the towns fined them. The death of Prince Maurice in 1625 and the rise of a tolerant party in Amsterdam changed everything. In 1630 the Amsterdam magistrates permitted the Remonstrants to build, provided the building could not be recognized as a church from the street; the meeting-house on the Keizersgracht, opened in September 1630, stood behind ordinary house fronts and seated a thousand. Uytenbogaert came home; Episcopius became the first professor of the Remonstrant seminary at Amsterdam in 1634. The Brotherhood is still called that.
documentedStories.caveat: The Antwerp meeting, the Confession and the Amsterdam permission are documented in the Brotherhood's records and the city's; the years of clandestine ministry are known mostly from the Remonstrants' own histories. The hidden church survives, as a concert hall.

movements.name: The Melkite Greek Catholic Split
movements.relationsSummary: When Patriarch Athanasius III died in 1724, the party at Damascus chose Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome. Constantinople consecrated a rival, Sylvester, instead. The see of Antioch split for good, and the Melkite Greek Catholic Church began. It is still alive today. The split took a shape seen before, in the Union of Brest and in the Maronites' union with Rome. The Orthodox side of the split stayed part of Orthodoxy under the Ottomans.

movements.name: The Ruthenian Uniate Church — Zamość to the Partitions
movements.why: A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands held the loyalty of most of the region's peasantry, and the Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it while importing Roman devotional practices into its Byzantine rite. When the partitions of Poland handed most of its people to Catherine II's Russia, which treated the union as an amputation to be reversed, forced-reversion campaigns from 1794 stripped away the great majority of its parishes within two years — leaving Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs funded the clergy's education, as the church's real survival zone.
movements.longDescription:
A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands — today's Ukraine and Belarus — was at its numerical height, holding the loyalty of most of the peasantry of the eastern Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it and also latinized it, importing Roman devotional practices into a Byzantine rite and settling its identity as something distinctly its own rather than a temporary arrangement. Then the political ground vanished: the partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 handed most of the church's people to Catherine II's Russia, which regarded the union as an amputation to be reversed, and campaigns of forced reversion from 1794 stripped it of the great majority of its parishes within two years. What survived did so in Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs raised the Greek Catholic clergy's status and paid for their education. And where the church became, over the following century, the carrier of Ukrainian national identity.

The Ruthenian church of the Carpathian lands had a union with Rome of its own, apart from the union of Brest. Nilles's heading dates the union at Uzhhorod to 1646. It dates the solemn confirmation to 1652.

In a petition of 15 January 1652, Greek-rite priests tell the pope that they were won back to Rome in the Latin church of the Uzhhorod castle, on 23 April. Their printed text names the year as 1649. Nilles notes that some read it as 1646, because the bishop of Eger who received them died in 1647.

Their earlier bishop at Mukachevo, they say, had left the union.

They joined on three terms. They would keep the Greek rite. They would have a bishop of their own choosing, confirmed by Rome. They would keep their church privileges. In their Latin, as the scan prints it: ritus graecae ecclesiae nobis servare Iice«t.

They asked Rome to confirm Peter Parthenius, the bishop they had chosen.

movements.legacy: The revival came as a wave, and by the 1970s the wave had passed. The fellowships had not. They lived on inside the Anglican churches of East Africa. They kept their meetings, their practice of confession and their hymn. The revival gave those churches a generation of African leaders. They were formed outside the control of missions. It also left a large body of testimony, and historians were slow to read it. Janani Luwum is honored among the twentieth-century martyrs on the west front of Westminster Abbey, unveiled in 1998.

documentedStories.title: The Mukono Expulsions
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: At the Anglican theological college of Uganda, the students touched by the revival rise before dawn to pray and preach to one another, confess their sins in public, and tell the staff they are not saved. The warden forbids the meetings; twenty-six refuse to stop and are sent down.
documentedStories.text: The revival that had begun at Gahini in Rwanda in the early 1930s had spread by 1941 through the Anglican church of Uganda in fellowship meetings whose members, the balokole, confessed their sins aloud, sang Tukutendereza Yesu, and asked everyone they met, clergy and Europeans included, whether they too were saved. At Bishop Tucker Memorial College at Mukono a group of students had joined the movement and had begun, in 1941, to hold meetings in the dormitories before the college's own morning prayers, at four or five o'clock, to preach to the other students and to tell members of staff that they were unconverted. The warden, J. C. Jones regarded this as a breach of discipline and of charity, and in October 1941 forbade the early meetings and the preaching. The balokole students answered that they could not obey a rule that forbade them to witness. Twenty-six were expelled, among them William Nagenda, who became the revival's most traveled African leader. The bishop, Cyril Stuart, supported the warden and then tried to hold the revival inside the church, ordaining some of the balokole and refusing to let the movement become a separate body, which its leaders did not want either. The expelled went out as lay evangelists and the fellowship grew faster than the college; by the 1950s the balokole were the church's most active members and some of its bishops, and the church that had expelled them had been remade by them.
documentedStories.caveat: The college's and the diocese's records and the balokole's own accounts document the expulsions; the accounts differ on the tone of the students' witness and on the warden's motives. The later reconciliation is documented in the church's own history and in the revival's.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop Who Walked to Rwanda
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The archbishop of Uganda is murdered by Amin's men after signing a protest against the killings, and the regime announces a car accident. The bishop of Kigezi, who had stood beside him, walks out of the country over the mountains with his wife and writes a book whose title is a decision.
documentedStories.text: Festo Kivengere had been converted in the revival as a schoolmaster, had preached with William Nagenda across the world, and in 1972 was made bishop of Kigezi, in the south-west of Uganda, the year after Idi Amin took power. In February 1977 the Anglican bishops of Uganda, led by Archbishop Janani Luwum, delivered to Amin a letter protesting the disappearances and the terror, and signed it. On 16 February Luwum and two cabinet ministers were arrested at a public rally at which Kivengere stood with him; that night Luwum was killed, and the government announced the next day that he and the ministers had died in a car accident. The bishops knew what had happened, and Kivengere was warned that he was next. On the night of 19 February he and his wife Mera drove toward the border, abandoned the car, and walked through the night over the Kigezi mountains into Rwanda. From exile he organized relief for Ugandan refugees, and within months had written a short book called I Love Idi Amin, in which he said that he had had to decide, in the days after Luwum's death, whether he would hate the man who had killed his archbishop, and had concluded that he could not, because Christ had died for Amin as for him. He returned to Kigezi after Amin fell in 1979, preached reconciliation through the wars that followed, and died in 1988. In 1998 Luwum's statue was set over the west door of Westminster Abbey.
documentedStories.caveat: Luwum's death and the regime's account are documented in the church's records and in the later inquiries; Kivengere's escape and his book are his own account and his wife's. The book's title was chosen by him and was controversial among Ugandans at the time, which the record shows.

movements.relationsSummary: The world's largest banned church - clandestine ordinations, bishops in the Gulag, emergence intact in 1989; a continuation of the Union of Brest. The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, dissolved in 1948, has its own entry.

documentedStories.title: A Council Without Bishops
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: With every Greek Catholic bishop already in prison, the NKGB assembles two hundred priests in Lviv to vote their church out of existence. The priest who chairs it is shot dead on a Lviv street two and a half years later.
documentedStories.text: In April 1945 the Soviet authorities arrested every bishop of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj among them. The following month an 'Initiative Group for the Reunion of the Greek Catholic Church with the Orthodox Church' announced itself, led by Havryil Kostelnyk, a respected Lviv priest, theologian and long-standing critic of Latin influence in his church, who had lost a son in the war. The group worked under the direction of the state security service, whose files, opened after 1991, record the arrangements. Priests who refused to join were arrested; some 800 signed. To give the gathering a semblance of episcopal presence, two members of the group, Mykhailo Melnyk and Antonii Pelvetsky, were secretly received into Orthodoxy and consecrated bishops in Kyiv in February 1946. On 8 to 10 March 1946, in St George's Cathedral in Lviv, 216 priests and 19 laypeople, with no bishop of their own church present, voted to annul the Union of Brest of 1596 and to join the Russian Orthodox Church. The church that had existed for three and a half centuries was declared not to exist. On 20 September 1948, after celebrating the liturgy at the Transfiguration Church in Lviv, Kostelnyk was shot dead in the street by a young man who then killed himself. The Soviet authorities blamed Ukrainian nationalists and the Vatican; the underground church suspected the security service of removing a man who knew too much. The question had not been settled by 2010.
documentedStories.caveat: The synod and the state's orchestration of it are documented in the NKGB and party files opened after 1991 and in the standard history built on them; the attendance figures are from those records. Kostelnyk's own motives, and who killed him, remain disputed, and the page states the competing accounts without choosing.

documentedStories.title: Eighteen Years, Then a Train to Rome
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An American editor carries a message from John XXIII to Khrushchev. Weeks later a Dutch monsignor collects a seventy-year-old metropolitan from Moscow and puts him on a train, on condition that he never go home.
documentedStories.text: Josyf Slipyj was arrested in April 1945, tried in secret and sentenced to eight years; when those ended he was sentenced again, and again, and by 1962 had spent seventeen years in camps and exile from Siberia to Mordovia, ordaining priests in secret when he could. In December 1962 Norman Cousins, the editor of the Saturday Review, visited Khrushchev as an unofficial go-between during the thaw after the Cuban missile crisis; he had been asked by John XXIII's circle to raise one specific matter, the metropolitan's release. Khrushchev agreed, on terms: Slipyj was to leave the Soviet Union and never return, and the release was to be presented as a humanitarian gesture, not a concession. On 26 January 1963 Slipyj was told he was free. Monsignor Jan Willebrands of the Secretariat for Christian Unity traveled to Moscow to collect him, and the two men went by train to Vienna, then on to Rome, arriving on 9 February. Slipyj had been permitted to bring a small suitcase; in it, among other things, was soil from the graves of his people in the camps. John XXIII received him at once. He was seventy, and he would live twenty-one more years in Rome, never returning to Lviv, holding together a banned church from outside and pressing at the Council and after it, without success, for the recognition of a Ukrainian patriarchate. His body was returned to St George's Cathedral in Lviv in 1992, when there was again a church to receive it.
documentedStories.caveat: The release is documented in Cousins's own account, in Willebrands's, in Slipyj's memoirs and in the Vatican's record; the detail of the soil rests on the accounts of those who received him. The terms Khrushchev set are as Cousins reported them. Slipyj's own experience of the camps is known from his own writing.

movements.name: Fundamentalism
movements.longDescription: The word arrived in 1920: Curtis Lee Laws, writing in the Watchman-Examiner, proposed calling those willing to do 'battle royal for the Fundamentals' fundamentalists, and the name stuck. The movement was older than the word. The Niagara Bible Conference had met annually from the 1870s until 1897 and adopted a fourteen-point creed in 1878; A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield published 'Inspiration' in the Presbyterian Review in April 1881, giving the doctrine of scripture its most exacting American statement. Between 1910 and 1915 twelve volumes called The Fundamentals were published, financed by Lyman Stewart and given away — around three million copies. The Presbyterian General Assembly adopted a five-point doctrinal deliverance in 1910. Then came the public defeats and the separations: the Scopes trial in July 1925, Princeton Seminary reorganized in 1929 with Westminster founded in answer, and new denominations of their own from the 1930s.

documentedStories.title: Bryan on the Lawn
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: On the seventh day of the Scopes trial, with the courtroom floor cracking under the crowd, the judge moves proceedings on to the lawn, and William Jennings Bryan takes the stand as an expert on the Bible. Five days after the verdict he is dead.
documentedStories.text: John Scopes, a young teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, had agreed to be prosecuted under the state's new law against teaching human evolution, in a test case the town's businessmen thought would bring visitors. It brought William Jennings Bryan, three times a presidential candidate and the country's best-known Christian layman, to assist the prosecution, and Clarence Darrow, its best-known agnostic, to the defense. The trial opened on 10 July 1925 in heat above a hundred degrees, and the judge ruled out the defense's scientific witnesses. On Monday 20 July, the court moved to a platform on the courthouse lawn, and Darrow called Bryan himself as a witness on the Bible. For two hours Darrow asked about Jonah, Joshua's sun, the date of the flood, and the six days of creation. Bryan held that the fish was a miracle and that he believed it; on the days he conceded that they might be periods, not twenty-four hours, and that he had not studied the matter, and the crowd, which had been his, laughed. The judge struck the testimony from the record the next morning. Scopes was convicted and fined a hundred dollars. Bryan stayed in Dayton to prepare the closing speech he had not been allowed to give; on Sunday 26 July he lay down for a nap after lunch and did not wake. The movement lost, that week, its public face, and drew from the loss the lesson that it would build its own institutions rather than argue in public.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial transcript is published and the exchange on the lawn is in it; the crowd's reactions are from contemporary press. The commonly repeated notion that Bryan was destroyed on the stand is a later dramatization, and the page follows the record, in which he was inconsistent, not humiliated, until he had gone home.

documentedStories.title: The Active Obedience of Christ
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Princeton scholar founds an independent mission board, is tried by his presbytery for it, is suspended from the ministry, founds a new church, and dies of pneumonia in North Dakota six months later, sending a last telegram about a doctrine.
documentedStories.text: J. Gresham Machen had left Princeton Seminary in 1929, when its board was reorganized to end conservative control, and founded Westminster Seminary in Philadelphia. In 1932 a lay commission's report, Re-Thinking Missions, questioned whether the Presbyterian mission enterprise should aim at conversion at all, and the novelist Pearl Buck said publicly that it should not. Machen concluded that the church's board could not be trusted with the gospel, and in June 1933 organized an Independent Board for Presbyterian Foreign Missions. The General Assembly of 1934 ordered all members to resign from it within ninety days. Machen refused, on the ground that no church court could order him to support a board he believed unfaithful. He was tried by the Presbytery of New Brunswick in early 1935; the court refused to hear his argument about the board's doctrine and found him guilty of disobedience and of disturbing the peace of the church, and suspended him from the ministry. The Assembly of 1936 upheld the sentence. On 11 June 1936 Machen and some thirty ministers constituted a new body, the Presbyterian Church of America, renamed the Orthodox Presbyterian Church in 1939 after a lawsuit over the name. That December, exhausted, he kept a speaking engagement in North Dakota against advice, caught pneumonia in the cold, and died in Bismarck on 1 January 1937, aged fifty-five. His last message, dictated to be telegraphed to his colleague John Murray, was: 'I'm so thankful for active obedience of Christ. No hope without it.'
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record and the Assembly's acts are published; the telegram is recorded by Machen's biographer and colleague. Historians of the movement note that the new church divided within the year over other questions, and that Machen's own relationship to the word fundamentalist was uneasy; the page does not smooth either.

documentedStories.title: Shall the Fundamentalists Win?
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Baptist preaching in a Presbyterian pulpit asks whether the fundamentalists will win. A publicist mails the sermon to every minister in the country, two General Assemblies try to make him conform, and he leaves rather than become a Presbyterian to stay.
documentedStories.text: Harry Emerson Fosdick was a Baptist, a professor at Union Theological Seminary, and since 1918 the regular preacher at First Presbyterian Church in New York, an arrangement the congregation had made and the presbytery tolerated. On 21 May 1922 he preached a sermon he called 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?', pleading for tolerance of ministers who did not hold the virgin birth, the inerrancy of scripture or a literal second coming as tests of fellowship, and saying that a church which drove them out would lose the coming generation. The congregation's publicist, Ivy Lee retitled it and mailed it to some 130,000 Protestant ministers. Clarence Macartney of Philadelphia answered with 'Shall Unbelief Win?', and the 1923 General Assembly, meeting in Indianapolis, directed the Presbytery of New York to see that the preaching at First Church conformed to the Westminster Confession, reaffirming five doctrines as essential. The presbytery exonerated Fosdick; a complaint went up again. The 1924 Assembly, at Grand Rapids, chose not to try him but to invite him to become a Presbyterian and so come under its discipline. He declined: he would not, he said, subscribe to a creed as a condition of preaching, and he resigned the pulpit, preaching his last sermon there on 1 March 1925 to a church filled beyond the doors. John D. Rockefeller Jr., a member of the congregation, then built him a church of his own on Riverside Drive, opened in 1930, where he preached until 1946 without a creed in the door.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermon text is published, the Assembly minutes record the votes, and Fosdick's own autobiography gives his side; Macartney's reply and the conservative accounts give the other. The page does not decide who won.

documentedStories.title: The Inaugural That Went to Trial
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A professor of biblical theology uses his inaugural lecture to say that the Bible has errors, that Moses did not write the Pentateuch, and that the church has made an idol of the book. The General Assembly vetoes his chair, tries him twice, and suspends him; his seminary walks out of the denomination.
documentedStories.text: Charles Augustus Briggs had taught Hebrew at Union Theological Seminary in New York since 1874 and was among the first American scholars to adopt the German historical criticism of the Old Testament. On 20 January 1891, inaugurated to a new chair of biblical theology, he delivered an address on 'The Authority of Holy Scripture' in which he said that the Bible contained errors, that Moses had not written the Pentateuch nor Isaiah the whole of Isaiah, that the church had turned the Bible into an idol as it had once turned the church and reason into idols, and that God speaks through reason and the church as well as through scripture. He said it with some heat. The Presbyterian General Assembly, which held a veto over Union's appointments under an agreement of 1870, refused to confirm him that May. The Presbytery of New York tried him for heresy and acquitted him in 1892; the prosecuting committee appealed, and in 1893 the Assembly at Washington, sitting as the church's highest court, found him guilty of teaching doctrines contrary to the Westminster standards and suspended him from the ministry. Union's directors had already voted to sever the seminary's relationship with the Assembly rather than surrender its chair, and did so in 1892; Briggs kept teaching there until his death in 1913. He was ordained an Episcopal priest in 1899. The conservative party had won the case and lost the seminary, which is roughly the shape the next century took.
documentedStories.caveat: The address is published, the trials are recorded in the Assembly's minutes and in the published trial proceedings, and the seminary's severance is in its own records. This story precedes the entry's window and is included because it is the background to the century's argument.

documentedStories.title: The Sunday After
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Five days after the towers fall, a Presbyterian congregation in Manhattan finds twice its usual number at the door, and its pastor preaches on the shortest verse in the Bible. Six years later he co-founds the coalition that gives the movement its confession.
documentedStories.text: Tim Keller had planted Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan in 1989, against the advice of people who told him that young professionals in New York would not come to a church with a Westminster confession; by 2001 some three thousand did each Sunday, meeting in rented auditoriums. On Sunday 16 September 2001, five days after the attacks, the congregation's numbers roughly doubled, with people standing along the walls of the Hunter College auditorium and a second overflow site. Keller preached on John 11, the raising of Lazarus, and on the two words 'Jesus wept'; his sermon, later published as 'Truth, Tears, Anger and Grace', said that Jesus did not explain Lazarus's death to Mary but wept with her, that anger at death was right because death was an enemy, and that grace was the only thing that would keep grief from turning to hate. The church spent the following months in the work of a parish in a wounded city, and much of the crowd stayed. In 2005 Keller and D. A. Carson gathered some forty pastors at Trinity Evangelical Divinity School to consider what a coalition around the gospel might be; in May 2007 The Gospel Coalition launched publicly with a Confessional Statement and a Theological Vision for Ministry that Keller had largely drafted, the New Calvinism's nearest thing to a common confession.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermon is published, the attendance is the church's account and contemporary reporting, and the coalition's founding documents are its own. He was a public figure, and the page does not assess his theology.

documentedStories.title: Lausanne, 1927
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Seventeen years after he conceived it at Edinburgh, an American missionary bishop opens the first world conference on the doctrines that divide the churches. Four hundred delegates from a hundred and eight churches argue for three weeks, and the Orthodox read a statement declining to vote.
documentedStories.text: Charles Brent, an Episcopal missionary bishop in the Philippines, had sat in the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910, from which doctrine had been excluded to keep the peace, and had come away convinced that the churches would have to talk about exactly what divided them or not be one at all. His church took up the proposal that autumn. The war intervened. On 3 August 1927 the first World Conference on Faith and Order opened in Lausanne with Brent presiding, some four hundred delegates from a hundred and eight churches, Protestant, Anglican, Old Catholic and Orthodox; Rome had declined. For three weeks the sections debated the gospel, the nature of the church, its common confession, its ministry and its sacraments, and produced reports that set agreements and disagreements side by side. On 18 August Archbishop Germanos of Thyateira read a statement for the Orthodox delegation: they had taken part gladly, they could accept the report on the gospel, and on the rest they would not vote, because the Orthodox church could not treat as open questions matters its councils had settled, and because a reunion built on compromise formulae would be no reunion. The conference received the statement without offense and printed it in full. That set the movement's method: to say plainly where the churches stood and to keep meeting. Brent died in 1929. The continuation committee he left became, twenty-one years later, half of the World Council of Churches.
documentedStories.caveat: The proceedings are published, including the Orthodox statement; the account follows them and the standard history of the movement. The page does not assess the theology of any report.

documentedStories.title: The Special Fund
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The World Council of Churches announces grants to nineteen organizations fighting racism, among them armed liberation movements in southern Africa. Eight years later a grant to a guerrilla army follows the killing of thirteen missionaries and children by that army's fighters, and churches begin to leave.
documentedStories.text: The Uppsala assembly of 1968, meeting weeks after the murder of Martin Luther King, who was to have preached to it, resolved that the churches must move from statements against racism to action. The Programme to Combat Racism was set up in 1969, and on 3 September 1970 its Special Fund announced its first grants: $200,000 to nineteen organizations, among them the African National Congress, ZANU and ZAPU in Rhodesia and SWAPO in Namibia, all engaged in armed struggle against white-minority or colonial rule. The grants were for humanitarian purposes, health, education and refugees, and were made without conditions; the council said the movements were the authentic voice of the oppressed and that it would not police money given in trust. Governments in Pretoria and Salisbury denounced it; so did member churches in Germany, Britain and America. In June 1978, at the Elim Pentecostal mission at Vumba in eastern Rhodesia, guerrillas of ZANLA, the armed wing of ZANU, killed eight British missionaries and four of their children; a ninth adult died of her wounds six days later. In August the Special Fund announced a grant of $85,000 to the Patriotic Front, the alliance of ZANU and ZAPU. The Salvation Army suspended its membership in the council that month and withdrew in 1981; the Presbyterian Church in Ireland withdrew in 1980; others reduced their contributions. The council did not rescind the grant. The program continued until 1994, when the movements it had funded were in government across the region, and both parties went on writing its history.
documentedStories.caveat: The grants, the killings and the withdrawals are documented in the council's own records, the withdrawing churches' published decisions and the contemporary press; the council's reasoning and its critics' are both stated. The page does not decide whether the grants were right.

movements.name: The Mennonites and the Amish
movements.sourcing: Thin for this period. The shelf holds later printings of older texts. The Martyrs Mirror of 1660 is here in an English edition of 1886. The Ausbund hymnal is here in Pennsylvania printings of 1846 and 1856. The Dordrecht Confession of 1632 is here in an Indiana manual of 1890. Their prefaces speak for the later church. From the 1700s, only the Ephrata chronicle tells of them, and it speaks from outside.
movements.floorNote: No question. Their Dordrecht Confession says that the Word became "flesh and man", born of the Virgin Mary.
movements.why: After 1650 the heirs of the Anabaptists became settled churches. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht gathered their martyrs into one great book, the Martyrs Mirror. He longed to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters". The book crossed the sea with his people. In Pennsylvania the Ephrata Brethren printed it in German, and in 1886 an English edition came out.
movements.longDescription:
After 1650 the heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists lived on as settled churches. Many were called Mennonites, after Menno Simons. Their Dordrecht Confession of 1632 stayed their rule of faith. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht published the Martyrs Mirror. It told of those "Who Baptized Only Upon Confession of Faith". In a prayer dated at Dort in 1659, he asked to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters".

In Pennsylvania the Mennonites wanted their great martyr book in German, not Dutch. The Ephrata community in Lancaster County did the work. Fifteen of its brothers were set to it, and the job took three years. The edition ran to 1300 copies.

The old hymn book of the Swiss Brethren, the Ausbund, was printed again and again in Pennsylvania. Its songs, the title says, were written in the prison at Passau. A Lancaster printing of 1856 calls itself the seventh in Pennsylvania. In 1886 Mennonite publishers brought out the Martyrs Mirror in English. English was spreading "year by year" among "our Mennonite people", its preface says.

In 1890 a manual from Elkhart set out the church's forms. A minister was chosen by lot. A slip with a verse from Proverbs went into one of several like books. The man whose book held it was ordained. Some congregations, "especially among the Amish and Russian Mennonites", chose by the members' vote instead.

The Mennonites also had a Russian chapter. Gerhard Wiebe, an elder of Bergthal, told it in 1900. A call came from Russia, he writes, and the first families left Prussia in 1788 or 1789. By 1790 eight villages had been settled. In the Molotschna colony thirty-nine villages were settled between 1804 and 1824. In the early 1870s the Mennonites read in the newspapers that they would be drafted. They sent men to St Petersburg. Many then left for America. Wiebe says his last brethren came from Russia in 1876.

The Hutterites, a church of their own, have a Russian chapter too. Josef Beck, who edited their chronicles, wrote in 1883 that single families who would not give up their fathers' faith went to Wischenka in Russia. In 1784, he says, part of the new converts fled to join them. The emigrants later moved on from Little Russia. Beck's preface says they went to the Crimea. His own note places their colony, Hutersthal, near the Sea of Azov, in the province of Taurida. In 1855, he says, the community stood under a grandson of the last bishop.

movements.name: Hugo Grotius
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Remonstrants and Dort. He sided with them but did not found that tradition, which began with the Remonstrance of 1610. English writers after 1660 name him; his legacy below says how.
movements.longDescription:
Grotius was a jurist on the Remonstrant side. In 1617 he published at Leiden a treatise on theology.

It answers Faustus Socinus, who denied that Christ's death satisfied divine justice. The treatise opens by promising to state first the doctrine which the church of Christ has defended 'with unshaken faith', as drawn from Scripture. It then sets that doctrine beside the view of Socinus. The Library holds it only in Foster's English.

Dort condemned the Remonstrants. Foster, who put the book into English, says Grotius shared the ban laid on his fellow Arminians. He adds that the English Arminians gave Grotius a kinder reception.

traces: Reformed writers who opposed him still borrowed from him. Heidegger took the idea of God as ruler of the universe to answer Socinus, and Turretin used the same phrase, though each meant something other than Grotius did.
The Dutch Arminians went another way. Episcopius, Curcellaeus and Limborch said God could forgive without any satisfaction, and put the need for the cross in God's will, not in a ruler's duty.

In England, Archbishop Tillotson stood first among the Arminians who largely took up his theory. In New England, Jonathan Edwards, then a pastor at New Haven, may have read him, since Grotius's example of Zaleucus turns up in Edwards's third sermon on the atonement, and Samuel Hopkins took up the governmental idea completely.
remembered: In 1692 Bishop Burnet wrote that Grotius's book on the truth of the Christian religion, with its notes, ought to be read and almost learned by heart.
Richard Baxter wrote against him in The Grotian Religion Discovered, in answer to Thomas Pierce, whose chief aim was to defend Grotius.
In Holland, once the Arminians were condemned at Dort, he shared the ban laid on them, and even as a commentator he was often met with prejudice and hostility.

uncertain: Why Grotius was condemned is not clear. Mosheim, who tells of the sentence, says the pretext and the charges are unknown to him. Hoogerbeets, the pensionary of Leyden, was imprisoned with him.
Grotius himself never calls his view the governmental theory. The name came later, and he speaks instead of God acting as ruler.
